ctx.x: That was very nice. (Recording interruption) Tell me a little bit about the Shim Sham Shimmy and how that reflected the personality of tap dancing.

Well, it reflected the personality of tap dancing because the chorus girls finally took an encore. Mr. Teddy Blackman -- he was the choreographer at that time at the Lafayette Theater, and sometimes he would go around into Connie's Carny's Inn and assist Mr. Clarence Robinson Robertson, which was another famous choreographer. He did shows for the Carny's Inn and the Cotton Club also -- mostly in the night clubs like Small's Paradise and sometime he did a lot of work for Ziegfield -- Florenz Ziegfield's…

dancer's night. Like when a celebrity -- a lot of celebrities used to come into Connie's Inn -- and they came to Harlem a lot at that time into these night clubs, and you may see anyone there, you see. You may see Dick Powell, the great singer, (Laughter) and some great band leader or somebody known dancers or whoever, you know. It was the master of ceremonies who made the show more entertaining, you see, because the dancer's night occurred after the first part of the show, like during the intermission, see. And…
